title: Nicotine and Alcohol: Effects, Hangovers, Patches and Risks
excerpt: Why alcohol makes you crave a cigarette or vape, whether nicotine makes you feel less drunk, how smoking affects hangovers and cancer risk, and whether patches, gum, and pouches are safe with drinking.
metaDescription: Why drinking makes you crave nicotine, whether it makes you less drunk, its effect on hangovers, and if patches, gum, or Zyn are OK with alcohol.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** nicotine and alcohol are one of the most common pairings there is, and that's not an accident. Each one makes the other feel better in the moment, which is why so many people who never smoke during the week find themselves bumming a cigarette or reaching for a vape after a few drinks. The combination isn't acutely dangerous for most healthy adults on a single night, but it does three things worth knowing about: it can make you feel less drunk than you are, it tends to make hangovers worse, and over years it multiplies the risk of certain cancers far beyond what either habit causes alone.

**The quick rules:** If you drink, try to keep nicotine out of the same session, or at least set a limit before you start. Don't use "I feel sober" as a signal after mixing the two, because nicotine can mask how impaired you are. If you're using nicotine patches, gum, or pouches to quit, they're fine to keep using on a night you drink, but drinking is one of the biggest triggers for slipping back to cigarettes, so plan for it. If you take a quit-smoking prescription like varenicline (Chantix) or bupropion (Zyban), talk to your doctor about alcohol before you drink.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before mixing alcohol with nicotine if** you have heart disease, high blood pressure, or an irregular heartbeat, you're pregnant, or you take a stop-smoking medicine such as varenicline or bupropion. **Get help right away (call 911, or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 in the US) if** someone has chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, fainting, a seizure, repeated vomiting, confusion, or trouble breathing, or if a child or pet may have swallowed vape liquid, nicotine gum, or pouches.

## Why Nicotine and Alcohol Go Together: The Brain Chemistry in Plain Words

The urge to smoke when you drink is real, and it has a clear basis in how both drugs act on the brain.

**Both drugs hit the brain's reward system.** Nicotine works by locking onto nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, which are switches spread throughout the brain. One effect of flipping those switches is a release of dopamine in the brain's reward pathway, the circuit that makes things feel satisfying and worth repeating. Alcohol also raises dopamine in that same pathway, partly through some of the same nicotinic receptors. When you take both together, the rewarding effects stack, and the pair can feel better than either one on its own.

**Each one seems to cover for the other's downsides.** Alcohol is a sedative. After a few drinks it slows you down and can make you sleepy. Nicotine is a stimulant. It raises your heart rate, sharpens attention for a short while, and pushes back against that drowsiness. Many people describe the combination as feeling more "up" and sociable than drinking alone. Going the other way, alcohol can take the edge off the jittery, slightly sick feeling some people get from nicotine, especially people who don't use it often.

**Alcohol makes the cravings stronger.** Lab studies that give volunteers alcohol and then measure their urge to smoke have consistently found that drinking increases craving, and that cigarettes are rated as more satisfying after alcohol. This effect shows up in light and occasional smokers too, not just in daily smokers. That's the science behind the "social smoker" who only ever smokes with a drink in hand.

**Habit and setting do the rest.** For a lot of people, drinking and smoking happen in the same places: bars, patios, parties, the back porch. Over time your brain learns to link the two, so the drink itself becomes a cue. That learned link is a big part of why drinking is one of the most commonly reported reasons people relapse after they quit smoking.

## Does Nicotine Make You More Drunk or Less Drunk?

This is one of the most common questions, and the answer has two parts: how drunk you *feel* and how drunk you actually *are*.

### You'll probably feel less drunk

Because nicotine is a stimulant, it can offset some of the sluggish, heavy feeling that alcohol brings on. That's why a cigarette or a hit from a vape can make you feel briefly more alert. The problem is that feeling more alert is not the same as being less impaired. Your reaction time, balance, and judgment are still affected by the alcohol in your blood. Nicotine doesn't clear any of it.

That mismatch matters for two reasons:

- **It can push you to drink more.** If you don't feel as drunk as you'd expect, it's easy to keep going. Researchers have suggested this "masking" effect is one reason people who smoke while drinking tend to drink larger amounts.
- **It can make you misjudge whether you're OK to drive.** Feeling clear-headed after a cigarette tells you nothing about your blood alcohol level. If you've been drinking, the rule is the same whether you smoked or not: don't drive.

### What happens to the alcohol in your blood is less clear

There is some interesting animal research here. A 2006 study in rats found that nicotine lowered blood alcohol levels, and the researchers linked this to nicotine slowing the rate at which the stomach empties into the intestine, where most alcohol is absorbed. Alcohol that sits longer in the stomach gets broken down a bit more before it reaches the bloodstream.

It would be a mistake to read too much into that. Rat studies don't always translate to people, the human data are limited, and the practical upshot isn't "nicotine sobers you up." If anything, the combination of a lower felt buzz plus a slower rise in blood alcohol could lead someone to drink more than they planned, only for the alcohol to catch up with them later in the night.

### Feeling sick from nicotine when drinking

Some people notice that a cigarette or vape they'd normally tolerate makes them dizzy, sweaty, or nauseous when they've been drinking. Occasional users call this getting "nic sick." It happens because nicotine raises heart rate, narrows blood vessels, and can trigger nausea, and you're layering that on top of alcohol, which already irritates the stomach and affects balance. People also tend to use far more nicotine than usual when they're drinking: chain-smoking, passing a vape around all night, or keeping pouch after pouch in. If you feel sick, stop the nicotine, sit or lie down somewhere safe, sip water, and give it time. Mild nicotine sickness usually passes within an hour or so once you stop.

## Nicotine and Hangovers: Does Smoking Make Them Worse?

Many people swear that the nights they smoke are the nights they feel worst the next morning. The research supports them.

A 2013 study of college students published in the *Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs* tracked drinking, smoking, and hangover symptoms day by day. It found that on days when students drank heavily, smoking more cigarettes was linked to worse hangovers the next day, even after accounting for how much they drank. In other words, two people drinking the same amount may not feel the same the next morning if one of them also smoked a pack.

Researchers don't know exactly why, but there are several believable explanations:

- **Poorer sleep.** Nicotine is a stimulant, and it can make it harder to fall asleep. In regular users, nicotine levels drop overnight, which can cause light, restless sleep as the body starts to crave it. Alcohol already wrecks the second half of the night by suppressing deep REM sleep early on and causing a rebound later. Stacking the two is a reliable way to wake up feeling unrested. Our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains the alcohol side of this in detail.
- **More inflammation and irritation.** Smoke irritates the throat and airways and adds a load of chemicals your body has to deal with. Many people wake up after a night of drinking and smoking with a sore throat, a cough, and a headache that feels different from an alcohol-only hangover.
- **More drinking.** As covered above, nicotine can make you feel less drunk, so people who smoke while drinking often drink more, and bigger nights mean worse mornings.
- **Nicotine withdrawal the next day.** If you only smoke when drinking, you probably won't feel withdrawal. If you smoke regularly, the morning after a big night can combine hangover symptoms with nicotine craving, irritability, and trouble concentrating, and it can be hard to tell which is which.

There's no good evidence that skipping nicotine prevents a hangover. It just appears to remove one thing that makes it worse.

## Your Heart and Blood Pressure

Both alcohol and nicotine affect your cardiovascular system, and they push in some of the same directions.

**Nicotine** speeds up your heart rate, raises blood pressure for a while after each dose, and narrows blood vessels. It does this whether it comes from a cigarette, a vape, a pouch, or gum, though smoking adds carbon monoxide and other combustion chemicals that are far harder on the heart and blood vessels than nicotine alone.

**Alcohol** has a more mixed short-term effect. It can relax blood vessels at first, but heavy drinking raises heart rate and, especially in the hours after a binge, can raise blood pressure. Large amounts of alcohol can also trigger episodes of irregular heartbeat, most often atrial fibrillation, in a pattern doctors have long called "holiday heart" because it shows up after weekends and holidays of heavy drinking.

Put together, a long night of drinking and heavy smoking or vaping can leave your heart racing, pounding, or skipping beats. For most healthy young people this is uncomfortable rather than dangerous, and it settles as both drugs wear off. If you have known heart disease, high blood pressure, or a history of irregular heartbeat, this combination deserves more caution, and it's worth asking your doctor about it. Our guide to [a racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) covers which symptoms are normal and which need care.

## The Long-Term Risk: Why Drinking and Smoking Together Multiplies Cancer Risk

This is the most important section for anyone who drinks and smokes regularly, even if it's mostly on weekends.

Alcohol and tobacco each raise the risk of cancers of the mouth, throat, voice box (larynx), and esophagus on their own. Used together, the risks don't simply add up. They multiply. Major health bodies, including the US National Cancer Institute, describe people who both drink and smoke as having a much higher risk of these cancers than people who do only one or the other.

Scientists think a few things explain this:

- **Alcohol acts like a solvent.** It may help the cancer-causing chemicals in tobacco smoke get into the cells lining the mouth and throat more easily.
- **Acetaldehyde.** When your body breaks down alcohol, the first by-product is acetaldehyde, which is classified as a carcinogen. Mouth bacteria can also make acetaldehyde from alcohol directly, and smoking appears to increase how much ends up in saliva.
- **Damage and repair.** Both alcohol and tobacco damage the lining of the mouth and throat, and alcohol may interfere with the body's ability to repair DNA damage.

**A special warning for people who flush when they drink.** If your face turns red after a drink or two, you may carry a common genetic variant (most common in people of East Asian descent) that slows the clearing of acetaldehyde. Research has linked this variant, combined with drinking, to a raised risk of esophageal cancer, and smoking adds to that risk. Our [complete guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) explains the genetics.

What about vapes and nicotine pouches? They don't produce tobacco smoke, so they avoid most of the combustion chemicals behind the multiplied cancer risk. That doesn't make them harmless, and long-term research on vaping is still limited, but the evidence for the drink-plus-smoke cancer link is strongest for burned tobacco.

## Nicotine Patches, Gum, and Pouches When You Drink

If you're using nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) to quit or cut down, you might wonder whether you need to take your patch off before a night out. Here's what's known.

### Is it safe to drink with a nicotine patch on?

For most healthy adults, yes. There's no known dangerous chemical interaction between the nicotine in a patch and alcohol, and US product labels for nicotine patches don't tell you to remove the patch before drinking. Keeping it on is usually the smarter move, because it keeps your nicotine level steady and makes it less likely you'll reach for a cigarette when the craving hits after a couple of drinks.

A few cautions:

- **Don't smoke or vape on top of the patch.** Drinking makes this tempting, and stacking nicotine sources is how people end up dizzy, nauseous, and with a pounding heart.
- **Watch your sleep.** Some people get vivid dreams or broken sleep from wearing a 24-hour patch overnight, and alcohol already disrupts sleep. If that's a problem, ask your pharmacist about a 16-hour patch or taking it off at bedtime.
- **Ask a doctor first if you have heart problems** or are pregnant, as you should with any NRT.

### Nicotine gum and lozenges

Nicotine gum and lozenges are absorbed through the lining of your mouth, and that absorption works best in a less acidic mouth. That's why the labels tell you not to eat or drink for about 15 minutes before using them and while you have them in. Acidic drinks, including beer, wine, soda, mixers, and coffee, can reduce how much nicotine you absorb. So if you're relying on gum to manage cravings on a night out, use it between drinks rather than with a drink in your hand, or a patch may simply work better for you that night.

### Nicotine pouches (like Zyn) and vapes

Pouches and vapes deliver the same drug, so the same principles apply. The specific risk with both is how easy it is to overdo it while drinking. With a cigarette, you finish it and there's a natural stopping point. With a vape or a tin of pouches there isn't, and people often use far more than usual over a long night. High-strength pouches in particular can cause nausea, hiccups, dizziness, and a racing heart in people who aren't used to them.

One safety point that gets overlooked: **keep vape liquid, pouches, and gum away from children and pets.** Swallowed nicotine can be seriously dangerous for them, and a late night out is exactly when these get left on a coffee table. If a child or pet may have swallowed any, call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) or your vet right away.

## Quit-Smoking Medicines and Alcohol

If you're taking a prescription to help you quit, alcohol is a bigger deal than with patches or gum.

**Varenicline (Chantix and generics).** In 2015 the FDA updated the warnings for varenicline after reports that some people had a reduced tolerance to alcohol while taking it, including becoming unusually drunk, acting aggressively or strangely, or having no memory of what happened. The FDA also noted rare reports of seizures. The advice in the label is to cut down on alcohol until you know how varenicline affects you. If you take it, talk to your prescriber about how much, if any, is reasonable for you.

**Bupropion (Zyban, also sold as Wellbutrin).** Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold, meaning it makes seizures more likely. Heavy drinking raises that risk, and so does suddenly stopping after drinking heavily on a regular basis. People on bupropion are usually advised to keep drinking to a minimum. Our [Wellbutrin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/wellbutrin-and-alcohol) goes into this in detail.

In both cases, don't stop or skip your medicine on a night you plan to drink without checking with your doctor first. The safer change is usually to drink less.

## Why Drinking Makes Quitting Nicotine So Hard

If you're trying to stop smoking or vaping, alcohol is one of the biggest obstacles you'll run into. The reasons are the same ones covered at the top of this article: alcohol increases cravings, makes nicotine feel more rewarding, lowers your resolve, and often puts you in places where other people are smoking.

Some practical ideas that help many people:

- **Plan the first few weeks with less drinking.** Many quit guides suggest cutting back on alcohol, or skipping it, for the first few weeks after you quit, while cravings are at their strongest.
- **Change the setting.** If your drinking always happens on the smoking patio, choose spots where smoking isn't part of the scene.
- **Keep your NRT on board.** A patch that's on before you start drinking helps more than trying to fight off a craving after three drinks.
- **Have something to do with your hands and mouth.** Gum (between drinks), a non-alcoholic drink in hand, or a toothpick sounds trivial, but it helps with the habit side of the urge.
- **Don't treat one slip as failure.** A cigarette on a night out doesn't undo your progress. Treat it as information about what triggered it, and plan for that next time.

In the US, free quit support is available by phone at **1-800-QUIT-NOW (1-800-784-8669)**, and smokefree.gov has free text and app programs.

## When to See a Doctor

> **When to see a doctor or get help**
>
> Most of the time, feeling a bit rough after a night of drinking and smoking or vaping passes on its own within a day. Get medical help if you notice any of these:
>
> - **Call 911 right away for:** chest pain or pressure, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle with rest, fainting, a seizure, severe trouble breathing, or someone who is very confused, can't be woken, or is vomiting while barely conscious. These can be signs of a heart problem or alcohol poisoning.
> - **Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) for:** a child or pet who may have swallowed nicotine liquid, gum, lozenges, or pouches, or an adult with severe vomiting, shaking, or a pounding heart after using a lot of nicotine.
> - **Book an appointment if:** you regularly get palpitations or a fluttering heartbeat after drinking, you have a cough or sore throat that lasts more than a few weeks, you notice a mouth sore or lump that doesn't heal within about two weeks, or you have trouble swallowing or a hoarse voice that won't go away.
> - **Talk to your doctor before drinking if:** you take varenicline or bupropion, you have heart disease or high blood pressure, or you're pregnant.

## A Practical Approach for Social Drinkers

If you drink socially and sometimes smoke or vape when you do, here's a sensible middle ground:

1. **Decide before you go out.** Set a limit on drinks and on nicotine before the first drink, when your judgment is at its best.
2. **Keep the two apart where you can.** Breaking the link between drinking and smoking is the single most useful thing for both your mornings and your long-term health.
3. **Pace yourself.** Alternate each alcoholic drink with water, and eat a proper meal before you start. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence behind them.
4. **Don't trust the "I feel fine" signal.** If you've been drinking, you're not OK to drive, no matter how alert nicotine makes you feel.
5. **Protect your sleep.** Stop nicotine a couple of hours before bed, drink water, and give yourself time to sleep it off.
6. **Watch for stacking stimulants.** Nicotine plus energy drinks or caffeine on top of alcohol makes it even harder to judge how drunk you are and is rough on your heart. See our guide to [caffeine and alcohol](/never-hungover/caffeine-and-alcohol) for why.

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that many people take on nights they drink. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with a small amount of human data. It's promising, but there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in people, and nothing suggests it reduces any of the risks of nicotine. It doesn't protect your heart from nicotine, doesn't lower your cancer risk from smoking, and doesn't make it safer to drive.

If you want to try DHM as one part of a sensible drinking routine, alongside eating, pacing, water, and keeping nicotine out of the picture, a popular choice is [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), and a budget-friendly option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take any prescription medication, check our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) or ask your pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

- Nicotine and alcohol both boost the brain's reward system, which is why drinking makes you want to smoke or vape, and why the pair feels better together than apart.
- Nicotine can make you feel less drunk without lowering your impairment. Don't use how alert you feel to decide whether you can drive or keep drinking.
- Smoking more on heavy-drinking nights is linked to worse hangovers, likely through poorer sleep, more irritation, and drinking more.
- Over years, drinking and smoking together multiply the risk of mouth, throat, and esophageal cancers far beyond either habit alone.
- Nicotine patches are generally fine to keep on when you drink; gum works poorly with a drink in your mouth; don't stack a patch with cigarettes or vaping.
- If you take varenicline (Chantix) or bupropion (Zyban), talk to your doctor before drinking.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is it bad to smoke or vape while drinking?**

For most healthy adults, one night of drinking and smoking isn't acutely dangerous, but the combination has real downsides. Nicotine can make you feel less drunk than you are, which can lead to drinking more, and smoking more on heavy-drinking nights is linked to worse hangovers. Over years, drinking and smoking together multiply the risk of mouth, throat, and esophageal cancers. If you have heart disease, high blood pressure, or take a quit-smoking medicine, talk to your doctor.

**Why do I want a cigarette when I drink?**

Alcohol and nicotine both raise dopamine in the brain's reward system, so each one makes the other feel more satisfying. Lab studies have found that drinking increases the urge to smoke and makes cigarettes more enjoyable, even in light and occasional smokers. Habit plays a big part too: if you usually smoke in the same places you drink, the drink itself becomes a cue for a cigarette.

**Does nicotine make you more drunk or less drunk?**

It usually makes you feel less drunk, because nicotine is a stimulant that offsets some of alcohol's sleepy, sluggish effects. But it doesn't lower your actual impairment. Your reaction time and judgment are still affected. A rat study found nicotine can slow how fast alcohol leaves the stomach, but there's limited human evidence, and nicotine does not sober you up. Never use how alert you feel to decide whether you can drive.

**Does smoking make a hangover worse?**

The evidence suggests it does. A 2013 study of college students in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs found that on heavy-drinking days, smoking more was linked to worse hangovers the next day, even after accounting for how much they drank. Likely reasons include worse sleep, more throat and airway irritation, and drinking more when smoking.

**Can you drink alcohol with a nicotine patch on?**

For most healthy adults, yes. There's no known dangerous interaction between a nicotine patch and alcohol, and keeping the patch on can help you resist cigarettes when drinking makes cravings stronger. Don't smoke or vape on top of the patch, as stacking nicotine can cause nausea, dizziness, and a racing heart. Ask your doctor first if you have heart problems or are pregnant.

**Can you use nicotine gum or Zyn pouches while drinking?**

You can, but nicotine gum and lozenges are absorbed less well in an acidic mouth, which is why their labels say not to eat or drink for about 15 minutes before and while using them. Beer, wine, soda, and coffee can all reduce absorption, so use gum between drinks. With pouches and vapes, the main risk is using far more than usual over a long night, which can cause nausea, dizziness, and a pounding heart.

**Can I drink alcohol while taking Chantix?**

Talk to your doctor first. In 2015 the FDA updated varenicline's warnings after reports of reduced alcohol tolerance, unusual or aggressive behavior, and memory loss in some people who drank while taking it, along with rare reports of seizures. The label advises cutting down on alcohol until you know how the medicine affects you.

**Do drinking and smoking together really increase cancer risk that much?**

Yes. Alcohol and tobacco each raise the risk of cancers of the mouth, throat, larynx, and esophagus, and used together the risks multiply rather than simply add up. Alcohol may help tobacco's cancer-causing chemicals get into cells, and alcohol's by-product acetaldehyde is itself a carcinogen. People who flush red when they drink appear to face extra risk of esophageal cancer.

**Does DHM help with nicotine and alcohol?**

There is no good evidence that DHM reduces any of the risks of combining nicotine and alcohol. It doesn't protect your heart from nicotine, lower your cancer risk, or make it safer to drive. DHM has promising research on alcohol metabolism, mostly from animal studies, but there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in people. Cutting down on nicotine when you drink is the step that makes the bigger difference.
